faq.q: Why does the diaphragm jerk in a hiccup?
faq.a: The nerves that run the diaphragm, mainly the phrenic and vagus nerves, get a burst of signals from a reflex centre in the brainstem. That makes the diaphragm contract suddenly, without you choosing to.
asks: Tell me about the diaphragm jerk

faq.q: Why do hiccups make a hic sound?
faq.a: Right after the sudden breath starts, the glottis, the gap between the vocal cords, snaps shut. Air hitting the closed door stops abruptly, and that makes the hic.
asks: Tell me about the vocal cords snapping shut
Where does the hic noise come from?

faq.a: Common triggers include eating too fast, a very full stomach, fizzy drinks, swallowing air, and sudden excitement. Each can irritate the nerves of the hiccup reflex.
asks: Tell me about the nerve getting triggered

faq.a: Scientists are not sure. One idea is that the reflex is left over from how unborn babies practise breathing movements, since babies hiccup in the womb; another is that it helps release swallowed air.
asks: Why do we have hiccups at all?

faq.a: Yes. Unborn babies hiccup in the womb, and newborns hiccup a lot. It is a normal reflex.

facts: In a hiccup the glottis closes about 35 milliseconds after the diaphragm contracts, producing the hic sound.
Babies hiccup before they are born.
